evidence_quotes.quote: This study aims to identify the actors who may contribute to the drinking water supply system in Indonesia. In addition, it also elucidates the tasks of each actor in accordance with what is stated in the Laws and regulations on drinking water supply in Indonesia.
Based on the extraction, there are seven regulatory documents in Indonesia regarding the drinking water supply system:

We used the Laws and regulations on drinking water supply as the data sources in this study to serve as the primary statutory instruments that govern the provision of drinking water supply in Indonesia. We focused on the actors stated in the Laws and regulation and their duties and responsibilities.

The results show that the instruments for drinking water supply are in a prominent position than instruments for its distribution. Only 3 of 19 instruments are identified for drinking water distribution: guideline, standard operational procedure, and master plan.
One limitation of this study is that it only focuses on the study of Laws and regulation– document study. It would be preferable if further research could be conducted to analyze the practices.

criterion_notes.c1: Although topically situated in Indonesia's drinking water supply sector, the paper does not examine actual household or community water or sanitation service access; it only inventories statutory actors and formal tasks written in national and ministerial regulations.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, this study would pass (plain=yes) because it examines Indonesian laws, government/ministerial regulations, and institutional responsibilities in the drinking water supply system. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, however, it fails (narrow=no): the paper conducts a broad macro-governance inventory mapping 21 actor categories to 19 general statutory tasks (such as guideline making, coaching, training, facilitation, master planning, construction, and unanalysed task labels like license approval and fare determination) rather than examining how a specific rule-type mechanism directly governs household or community service access. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper is still excluded because it lacks empirical evidence and reports no service access outcome.
criterion_notes.c3: Purely a desktop doctrinal/document study coding the text of Indonesian laws and regulations from peraturan.go.id in NVivo (158 water-related laws/regulations narrowed to 7 drinking water supply regulations). As the authors explicitly state in the Conclusion, the study only examines laws and regulations on paper and does not empirically investigate real-world implementation or practices (Exclusion Criterion 1 / E05).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports no empirical outcome relevant to water access, connection, service availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion. The reported results consist solely of a list of 7 regulations and a table of 21 statutory actors and 19 formal tasks, while mentions of service 'blank spot areas' and reliability gaps in the Discussion are unmeasured commentary.
criterion_notes.c5: The unit of analysis is statutory/regulatory text (7 Indonesian regulations), with no household, community, settlement, or utility sample and no identifiable empirical exposure-outcome relationship for service access.
criterion_notes.c6: The full text is written in English.

study_design: Statutory/regulatory document content analysis (doctrinal mapping in NVivo)
population_and_sample: Indonesian statutory and regulatory documents from peraturan.go.id (158 laws and regulations with 'air (water)' in the title, narrowed to 7 drinking water supply system regulations); no household, community, or utility sample
exposure: Statutory actor and task provisions in 7 Indonesian drinking water supply regulations (no empirical exposure measured)
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Despite 'implementation' in the title, the paper is strictly a doctrinal/statutory document study that codes 7 Indonesian drinking water supply regulations in NVivo to catalogue formal actors (21 categories) and statutory duties/instruments (19 tasks, such as guidelines, master plans, coaching, and licensing). As the authors note in the Conclusion, it focuses solely on laws and regulations on paper without examining empirical implementation practices, and it reports no empirical household or community water access outcome (also failing c1, c2 narrow rule-type scope, c4, and c5).
